p.src: A Periodic Line as a Regulator

u.src: A Periodic Line as a Regulator
en: A Periodic Line as a Regulator

p.src: Begin with a line segment of length $L$, but identify its two ends. A particle that leaves at one end reappears at the other. This is equivalent mathematically to motion on a circle, although we need not imagine the particle literally travelling around a physical ring. The construction is a regulator: it makes momentum discrete and normalization ordinary, and the infinite line is recovered by taking $L$ to infinity.

p.src:
Momentum eigenfunctions are plane waves. Restoring units before simplifying the notation, $e^{ipx/\hbar}=e^{ikx},
  \qquad
  k:=\frac{p}{\hbar}.$ Thus $k$ is the wave number, while the physical momentum is $p=\hbar k$. On one period, a normalized plane wave is $\psi_k(x)=\braket{x}{k}_{\mathrm{box}}
    =\frac{e^{ikx}}{\sqrt{2\pi r}},
  \qquad 0\leq x<2\pi r.$

p.src:
Periodicity now quantizes the wave number: $\begin{aligned}
  e^{ik(x+2\pi r)}&=e^{ikx},\\
  e^{i2\pi rk}&=1,\\
  k&=\frac{n}{r},
  \qquad n\in\mathbb Z.
  \end{aligned}$ The allowed values are separated by $\Delta k=\frac{1}{r}.$ As $r$ grows, the spectrum becomes dense. A dense quantum spectrum is not by itself a classical limit; it is only the continuum limit of this kinematical basis.

p.src: Dyads and the Resolution of Identity

u.src: Dyads and the Resolution of Identity
en: Dyads and the Resolution of Identity

p.src:
An inner product such as $\braket ab$ is a number. Reversing the order creates a different kind of object: $\ket b\bra a.$ This outer product, or dyad, is an operator. Acting on a third vector, $\bigl(\ket b\bra a\bigr)\ket c
    =\braket ac\,\ket b.$ The bra extracts the component of $\ket c$ along $\ket a$, and the ket places that coefficient along $\ket b$.

p.src:
For an abstract state $\ket\psi$, define $\psi(x):=\braket x\psi,
  \qquad
  \widetilde\psi(k):=\braket k\psi.$ They are not two states. They are the components of one state in two different bases. The change-of-basis kernel is $\braket xk=\frac{e^{ikx}}{\sqrt{2\pi}},
  \qquad
  \braket kx=\frac{e^{-ikx}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.$

p.src:
The operator rules display the same reciprocity. In the position representation, $\begin{aligned}
  \hat X\psi(x)&=x\psi(x),\\
  \hat K\psi(x)&=-i\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\psi(x).
  \end{aligned}$ In the wave-number representation, $\begin{aligned}
  \hat K\widetilde\psi(k)&=k\widetilde\psi(k),\\
  \hat X\widetilde\psi(k)&=
    i\frac{\partial}{\partial k}\widetilde\psi(k).
  \end{aligned}$ The physical momentum operator is $\hat P=\hbar\hat K$.

p.src: Wave Packets and the Classical Bridge

u.src: Wave Packets and the Classical Bridge
en: Wave Packets and the Classical Bridge

p.src: At this stage, the operators have been named position and momentum, but the connection with classical motion has not yet been proved. The bridge is a wave packet. Its magnitude is concentrated near some position $x_0$, and its Fourier transform is concentrated near some wave number $k_0$. A typical form is $\psi(x)=f(x-x_0)e^{ik_0x},$ where $f$ is a smooth localized envelope. The oscillations inside the envelope carry the approximate momentum, while the envelope locates the particle.

p.src: Under a sufficiently smooth potential, a narrow packet can retain its integrity for a useful interval. Its center moves through position space, and the center of its momentum distribution moves through momentum space. The theorem promised in the lecture is the Ehrenfest relation: under the conditions in which the packet remains narrow, these expectation values approximately obey the classical equations of motion. The packet may also spread or distort, so the classical description is an approximation, not a new postulate.

p.src: A classical light wave travelling along the $z$-axis has electric and magnetic fields transverse to its motion and perpendicular to one another. For a plane wave they oscillate in phase. The polarization direction is defined to be the direction in which the electric field oscillates; the opposite direction along the same axis is not a different linear polarization.

p.src: A wire-grid polarizer makes this physical. If its conducting wires are vertical, a vertical electric field drives currents in the wires. Those currents reflect or absorb that component. A horizontal electric field cannot drive a horizontal current because no conducting path runs that way, so it is transmitted. Thus the transmission axis is perpendicular to the wires. More generally, an ideal polarizer transmits the electric-field component along one axis and removes the orthogonal component.

p.src: Preparation and Measurement

u.src: Preparation and Measurement
en: Preparation and Measurement

p.src: A photon that emerges from an ideal vertical polarizer is vertically polarized. If it then meets a second vertical polarizer, it passes with probability one. If it meets a horizontal polarizer, it is blocked with probability one. The first apparatus prepares a state; the second tests it. The same physical device can therefore serve as a state preparer or as a measurement apparatus, depending on its role in the experiment.

p.src: Nothing prevents us from rotating a polarizer by $45^\circ$. A photon that emerges from it is neither in $\ket x$ nor in $\ket y$, but an $x$- or $y$-oriented test gives either result with equal probability. The normalized state is $\ket{+}=\frac{\ket x+\ket y}{\sqrt2}.$ The orthogonal linear polarization is $\ket{-}=\frac{\ket x-\ket y}{\sqrt2}.$

p.src:
The Born rule confirms the equal probabilities: $\begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{Prob}(y|+)
    &=\left|\braket y+\right|^2
      =\left|\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
        \bigl(\braket yx+\braket yy\bigr)\right|^2\\
    &=\frac12,\\
  \operatorname{Prob}(x|+)&=\frac12.
  \end{aligned}$ For $\ket-$, one amplitude changes sign, but its absolute square is again $1/2$. Amplitudes carry signs and phases; probabilities do not retain them directly.

p.src: The eigenvectors of $\hat P_{xy}$ are $\ket x,\ket y$; those of $\hat P_{45}$ are $\ket+,\ket-$. No nonzero vector is an eigenvector of both operators. p.src: The probability for a particular eigenstate $\ket a$ is obtained directly from the overlap, $\operatorname{Prob}(a|\psi)=\left|\braket a\psi\right|^2.$ One does not first apply the observable to $\ket\psi$ and then square an eigenvalue. The observable identifies the possible values and the eigenvectors associated with them; the state’s overlaps with those eigenvectors determine the probabilities.

p.src:
The numerical labels $+1$ and $-1$ are a convention. We could record $1$ and $0$, or any two distinct real numbers, provided the convention is used consistently. Choosing $1$ and $0$ produces the projector $\Pi_x=\ket x\bra x
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    1&0\\
    0&0
  \end{pmatrix}.$ For a normalized state $\ket\psi$, $\begin{aligned}
  \bra\psi\Pi_x\ket\psi
    &=\bra\psi x\rangle\braket x\psi\\
    &=\left|\braket x\psi\right|^2.
  \end{aligned}$ The expectation value equals the probability, but the result of one projector measurement is still $1$ or $0$.

p.src: An observable is therefore inseparable from a specified experimental question. The polarizer orientation fixes the eigenvectors, the notebook convention fixes the eigenvalues, and one interaction yields one recorded event. Repetition reveals the probabilities. In this two-state example, the abstract language of vectors, operators, incompatible bases, and Born amplitudes has become a concrete laboratory procedure.
